entries.title: The Illness
entries.text: Erol's mind had been failing for months. The official fever was a curtain.

entries.title: No Public Body
entries.text: The court was not allowed to look at the king for long. What they were protected from is still argued.

entries.title: The Physicians Silenced
entries.text: Only Pell remained in the room. The other doctors were sent away while Erol could still give orders.

entries.title: The Dose
entries.text: Nessa Grey saw Mira with the king's medicine on the last night. She did not see what the dose was for.

entries.title: A Request
entries.text: Erol asked not to become the man the illness was making. Whether that was a plea for mercy or a trap depends on who is speaking.

entries.title: Pell's Silence
entries.text: The physician's refusal to describe the night is itself a kind of testimony. He promised Erol.

entries.title: Contradictory Orders
entries.text: A dying king produced papers that cannot all be true. Fear, not a single plan, wrote them.

entries.title: The Accusation
entries.text: Mira accused Ethan of assault. Erol offered execution or exile. Ethan chose exile and silence.

entries.title: Inside the Chambers
entries.text: Ethan was in Mira's rooms that night. The official story does not explain why.

entries.title: The Argument
entries.text: Accounts agree that a private dispute concerned Erol’s possible illegitimate child. Mira describes being grabbed; Ethan describes restraining her during a blow. A corridor witness heard shouting, not every act in the room. The later accusation remains politically potent and cannot be settled by a convenient slogan.

entries.title: Erol Believed Her
entries.text: The king chose his wife over his brother. Whether he believed her, or needed to, is not in the sentence.

entries.title: The Road
entries.text: Ethan did not write. He became a hired sword and a story soldiers told when they were drunk.

entries.title: The Men Who Remember
entries.text: Old companies still measure other commanders against Ethan, which is a kind of loyalty and a kind of problem.

entries.title: Lysa
entries.text: A servant at a hunting lodge, dead in childbirth. The child lived. The payments started.

entries.title: The Payments
entries.text: House Maren received royal money for twenty-three years. It stopped when Erol died.

entries.title: Master Ren
entries.text: The tutor who visited Arlo was Erol under another name. They played chess. The king did not say he was a king.

entries.title: The Lodge
entries.text: Someone from the old lodge remembers the pregnancy and the order to forget it.

entries.title: Evelyne's Hatred
entries.text: Lady Maren raised the boy and despised the king for using her house as a cupboard.

entries.title: The Last Words
entries.text: Erol's letter to Maren refuses to call Arlo his son and refuses to call him nothing.

entries.title: An Unfinished Act
entries.text: Erol asked how a bastard might be legitimised. He did not complete it.

entries.title: Tomas's Fear
entries.text: Lord Maren believes the truth will get Arlo killed faster than the lie.

entries.title: The One Queen
entries.text: Aria became queen at twenty-six after plague killed her father and brothers. She defeated rebellious lords and ruled for twenty-seven years. Her roads, courts and restrictions on private armies endured even while later commentators called her an exception.

entries.title: The Precedent
entries.text: The original writ invokes the need to preserve the realm as well as descent. It offers a legal argument for extraordinary succession, rather than proving that every able person can inherit.

entries.title: Not Her Sex
entries.text: The old argument against Mira is not only that she is a woman. It is that she is not Valen blood.

entries.title: Aria's Father
entries.text: A surviving scrap questions Aria’s parentage. Its existence is established; the allegation is not. Revealing it can unsettle bloodline politics without turning an unverified historical rumour into fact.

entries.title: The First Blessing
entries.text: The Flame blessed Aria because the High Keeper of that age feared a battlefield more than a queen.

entries.title: Order
entries.text: Alistair's case is not blood. It is that Nezrel collapses when no one is willing to be hated.

entries.title: The Informant
entries.text: A household clerk passed reports of Erol’s decline to Stormhold. The reports gave Alistair advance knowledge, not proof of a role in the king’s death.

entries.title: Burned Letters
entries.text: Alistair burned the correspondence. He wanted the information and not the proof that he had wanted it.

entries.title: One Letter Kept
entries.text: A single page survived the fire. It is enough to show he knew Erol was dying.

entries.title: The Offer
entries.text: Storm's first move was not a march. It was a marriage offer that was also a threat.

entries.title: Dictated
entries.text: Erol dictated a final document. Pell heard pieces. Nessa heard the end.

entries.title: Vanished
entries.text: The testament was not in the chamber by morning. No one agrees who took it.

entries.title: The Remembered Line
entries.text: The crown must belong not to the one born nearest it, but to the one who can keep Nezrel whole.

entries.title: Every Claimant Hears Themselves
entries.text: The line can be made to mean Mira, Ethan, Arlo, Alistair, or no king at all.

entries.title: Three Papers
entries.text: Separate authentic instructions favour Ethan, a legitimised Arlo, and Mira's emergency power. They were not written on the same day.

entries.title: The Document Itself
entries.text: The recovered testament compares an uncertain succession with the duty to preserve Nezrel. It does not cleanly appoint a single heir. Authentication gives the living a common document to argue from, not a dead man’s answer to every question.

entries.title: The Forgotten Passage
entries.text: A wet drain beneath Caerlyn’s east wall served as a discreet royal exit. A later claimant can independently hear of it from a working mason; the Chronicle opens an opportunity, not a shared memory.

entries.title: The Tutor's Name
entries.text: Records and household memories identify Master Ren as Erol. In another campaign the name may arrive through a horse-seller who visited Maren, giving that claimant a reason to investigate.

entries.title: The Northern Clerk
entries.text: The clerk’s reports have left traces in accounts and correspondence. Later courts may discover those traces through their own inquiries.

entries.title: A Kinder Version of the Night
entries.text: A less damning account of the chambers encounter has reached the roads. It creates a chance to hear a witness in another campaign. It does not certify every detail of Ethan’s account.

categories.title: The Work That Outlived the War

entries.title: The Open Granary
entries.text: A public account linked grain purchase, delivery and rationing. A rule survived because ordinary households could check whether it was being obeyed.

entries.title: The Mothers’ Petition
entries.text: Mira heard people whose grief had been used as a public accusation. Their petition changed the duties of a household without pretending grief could be repaired by a crown.

entries.title: Names on the Roll
entries.text: Ethan’s pension settlement made the returned veterans people with households again, rather than a legend’s unpaid army.

entries.title: Lysa’s Name
entries.text: Arlo recovered his mother’s remembered wishes and chose how to preserve them. A parent’s life became more than a proof of royal blood.

entries.title: The Northern Compact
entries.text: Alistair allowed inspection of mine safety and levy obligations. The settlement made order answerable to people who had lived beneath it.

entries.title: The Water Agreement
entries.text: Upstream and downstream villages accepted a shared water schedule. The agreement took cooperation beyond the banner that first sponsored it.

entries.title: The Salt Convoy
entries.text: Escorted merchants delivered supplies under a written loss-sharing agreement. Trade became a promise that could be measured at the quay.

entries.title: An Oath Kept
entries.text: A promise to spare prisoners survived a difficult victory. Witnesses remembered restraint because the ruler had enough power to choose otherwise.
